saints.name: Sts. Protus and Hyacinth
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two early Roman martyrs, remembered as brothers, whose tombs on the Old Salarian Way were honoured from the earliest centuries…
biography: Protus and Hyacinth were Roman martyrs of the persecution of Valerian, about the years 257-259. Later legend made them brothers and household servants of St. Eugenia, scourged and beheaded for refusing sacrifice; what is certain is their ancient cult, for the Roman calendar of 354 already kept their feast on 11 September.

They were buried in the cemetery of Basilla on the Old Salarian Way, in what was later called the catacomb of St. Hermes. There in 1845 the archaeologist Giuseppe Marchi found the grave of Hyacinth still sealed, its inscription intact and, within, charred bones wrapped in costly stuffs -- the martyr, it seems, had died by fire. Part of the emptied tomb of Protus lay nearby.

The discovery, unique among the Roman martyrs, confirmed the testimony of the ancient itineraries and pilgrim guides. Their feast on 11 September stood in the Roman calendar until the reform of 1969, and their names are still proclaimed in the Roman Martyrology on that day.
saints.knownFor: Their witness of blood in early Roman persecution.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 11 September
